Trail Physics · Unit 2: Understanding Motion · Module 6

Projectile Motion

Motion in two dimensions: why horizontal and vertical motion are independent, and how to predict flight time, height and range.

Lesson coming

The question

Why does a little more speed send you so much farther off a jump?

The physics

  • Two-dimensional motion
  • Horizontal and vertical velocity
  • Independence of motion
  • Maximum height
  • Flight time
  • Range
  • Trajectory

The math

  • vx = v₀ cos θ
  • vy = v₀ sin θ
  • x(t) = x₀ + vx·t
  • y(t) = y₀ + vy·t − ½gt²

About the model: Jump Lab uses an idealized projectile model: no air resistance and no rider movement in the air.

Learning objectives

  • Split a takeoff velocity into horizontal and vertical components
  • Explain why horizontal and vertical motion are independent
  • Calculate flight time, maximum height and horizontal range
  • Predict where a rider lands, using the trajectory equations
  • Explain how takeoff speed and angle change a trajectory

Helps to know first: Motion in One Dimension, Vectors.

The mountain biking connection

Once a rider leaves the lip of a jump, only gravity acts on them (in the ideal model). Horizontal speed stays the same, vertical speed changes steadily, and the path is a parabola.
